Chapter 4: Two Types of Investors—Defensive and Enterprising Approaches
Let’s dive into one of the most important ideas in value investing: not every investor is the same. Think about it—some folks love digging into numbers and tracking the market, while others just want a simple, steady way to grow their money.
That’s why there are two main paths you can take: the defensive, or passive, approach, and the enterprising, or active, approach.
If you see yourself as a defensive investor, you’re probably looking for simplicity and safety. Maybe you don’t have the time or interest to analyze every company out there—and that’s perfectly okay. Your main goal? To avoid big mistakes and get steady, reasonable returns, without a lot of stress.
Here are a few habits that really help defensive investors:
First, broad diversification. That just means spreading your money across different types of investments—like a mix of stocks and bonds—so you’re not putting all your eggs in one basket.
Next, focus on quality. Stick with well-established companies that have strong finances.
It’s also smart to review your portfolio every now and then, but don’t feel like you need to react to every little move in the market.
And here’s a big one—don’t try to time the market. Predicting short-term swings or chasing hot trends can be risky and exhausting.
For example, imagine someone who invests in a handful of big, stable companies, adds some government or high-quality corporate bonds, and checks their investments once or twice a year. They only make changes when something important happens. Easy, right?
Now, on the other side, we have the enterprising investor. If you’re willing to spend more time and energy, and you like the challenge of finding hidden gems, this approach might be for you.
The enterprising investor is all about putting in the work—studying financial reports, keeping up with industry trends, and really getting to know the companies they invest in.
They’re always on the lookout for bargains, especially in stocks that most people are ignoring or that have fallen out of favor.
This approach also means keeping a close eye on your investments and being ready to make changes when things shift.
But maybe most importantly, it takes strict discipline. Enterprising investors avoid wild speculation and stick to a clear, well-defined plan.
Picture someone who spends a few hours each week digging into small companies the market has overlooked, searching for those rare deals trading below their true value. It’s hard work—but for the right person, it can really pay off.
So, which path is best? Well, both can lead to success, but they each call for a different mindset and level of commitment.
The real trick is picking the approach that fits your own abilities, interests, and temperament—and then sticking with it, consistently and with discipline.
